claim: Every Lambda function must have an execution role, and at a minimum the role needs access to Amazon CloudWatch because functions log to CloudWatch Logs by default; the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole managed policy satisfies this.
question: Does every Lambda function need an execution role, and what is the minimum it must allow?

values.display: must have an execution role
values.spoken: every function needs an execution role

values.display: AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
log to CloudWatch Logs by default

evidence.quote: Every Lambda function must have an execution role. At a minimum, your execution role must have access to Amazon CloudWatch because Lambda functions log to CloudWatch Logs by default. You can attach the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole managed policy to your execution role to satisfy this requirement.

claim: Lambda automatically assumes the execution role when the function is invoked, and the role's trust policy must name the Lambda service principal (lambda.amazonaws.com) as a trusted service.
question: What must an execution role's trust policy contain so that Lambda can use it?

values.display: lambda.amazonaws.com
Lambda automatically assumes your execution role

evidence.quote: Lambda automatically assumes your execution role when you invoke your function.
In order for Lambda to properly assume your execution role, the role's trust policy must specify the Lambda service principal (lambda.amazonaws.com) as a trusted service.

claim: When a user accesses a Lambda resource, Lambda evaluates both the user's identity-based policies and the resource-based policy, but when an AWS service such as Amazon S3 calls the function, Lambda considers only the resource-based policy.
question: Which policy decides whether an AWS service such as Amazon S3 may invoke a Lambda function?

values.display: Lambda considers only the resource-based policy
values.spoken: only the function's resource-based policy counts

values.display: considers both the user's identity-based policies

evidence.quote: When a user tries to access a Lambda resource, Lambda considers both the user's identity-based policies and the resource's resource-based policy. When an AWS service such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) calls your Lambda function, Lambda considers only the resource-based policy.

claim: A resource-based policy on a function can grant other AWS accounts, users, organizations and AWS services access to the function, and each statement can apply to the function, a version or an alias.
question: Who can a Lambda function's resource-based policy grant access to?

values.display: grant other AWS accounts, users, organizations, and AWS services
values.spoken: other accounts, organizations and AWS services

values.display: The Lambda function, version, or alias

evidence.quote: With resource-based permissions policies, you can grant other AWS accounts, users, organizations, and AWS services access to your Lambda functions.
Resource: The Lambda function, version, or alias you want the statement to apply to (you can also use a wildcard character to specify all of your function's versions and aliases)

claim: Individual permissions added with the console or the AddPermission API are single Allow statements that support only aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount and aws:PrincipalOrgID as condition keys; a full JSON policy (PutResourcePolicy) supports all IAM global condition keys, multiple principals and explicit Deny statements.
question: What can a full JSON resource-based policy do that AddPermission cannot?

values.display: add single Allow statements
only a limited set of condition keys
create explicit Deny statements

evidence.quote: Individual permissions – Use the console or AddPermission API action to add single Allow statements. Individual permissions support only a limited set of condition keys (aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount, and aws:PrincipalOrgID).
With a full JSON policy, you can use the complete range of IAM global condition keys, add multiple statements with multiple principals, and create explicit Deny statements.

claim: Using put-resource-policy replaces any existing resource-based policy on the function, including permissions added with add-permission, while add-permission appends a statement without overwriting.
question: Does put-resource-policy add to or replace a Lambda function's existing resource-based policy?

values.display: replaces any existing resource-based policy
Adds a statement to the existing policy without overwriting

evidence.quote: Using put-resource-policy replaces any existing resource-based policy on the resource. If the resource already has permissions defined with add-permission, put-resource-policy overwrites them.
add-permission / AddPermission – Adds a statement to the existing policy without overwriting.

claim: A function URL's AuthType is either AWS_IAM, where IAM authenticates and authorizes requests using the principal's identity policy and the function's resource-based policy, or NONE, where Lambda performs no authentication but the resource-based policy must still grant public access.
question: What are the two auth types of a Lambda function URL, and what does each mean?

values.display: AWS_IAM
Lambda doesn't perform any authentication
must grant public access

evidence.quote: AWS_IAM – Lambda uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) to authenticate and authorize requests based on the IAM principal's identity policy and the function's resource-based policy.

NONE – Lambda doesn't perform any authentication before invoking your function. However, your function's resource-based policy is always in effect and must grant public access before your function URL can receive requests.

claim: If a function's resource-based policy does not grant lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction, callers get a 403 Forbidden error from the function URL, even when the auth type is NONE.
question: Why can a public (auth type NONE) Lambda function URL still return 403 Forbidden?

values.display: 403 Forbidden
even if the function URL uses the NONE auth type

evidence.quote: If a function's resource-based policy doesn't grant lambda:invokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions, users get a 403 Forbidden error code when they try to invoke your function URL. This occurs even if the function URL uses the NONE auth type.

claim: A function can mount an Amazon EFS file system to a local directory, so the function code can access and modify shared resources safely and at high concurrency; the function connects to the file system over the local network in a VPC.
question: How can several Lambda functions share files that persist between invocations?

values.display: mount an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system
access and modify shared resources safely
over the local network in a VPC

qualifiers.scope: Lambda function with an Amazon EFS file system
qualifiers.condition: the function connects to a VPC

evidence.quote: You can configure a function to mount an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system to a local directory. Amazon EFS is a serverless file system that scales automatically with your workloads. With Amazon EFS, your function code can access and modify shared resources safely and at high concurrency.
A function connects to a file system over the local network in a VPC.

claim: For Lambda, create the EFS file system with a mount target in every Availability Zone the function connects to, use at least two Availability Zones for performance and resilience, and allow NFS traffic (port 2049) in the security groups of the function and the mount targets.
question: How should an EFS file system be set up so that a Lambda function can use it reliably?

values.display: a mount target in every Availability Zone
values.spoken: a mount target in every Availability Zone

values.display: use at least two Availability Zones
NFS traffic (port 2049)

qualifiers.scope: Amazon EFS file system used by Lambda

evidence.quote: Create a file system in Amazon EFS with a mount target in every Availability Zone that your function connects to. For performance and resilience, use at least two Availability Zones.
Ensure that NFS traffic (port 2049) is allowed by the security groups used by the function and mount targets.

claim: If the EFS file system has a user-configured IAM policy, the function's execution role needs the matching elasticfilesystem permissions (included in the AmazonElasticFileSystemClientReadWriteAccess managed policy) and the permissions required to connect to the file system's VPC.
question: Which permissions does a Lambda execution role need to use an Amazon EFS file system?

values.display: AmazonElasticFileSystemClientReadWriteAccess
values.spoken: the EFS client read-write managed policy

values.display: permissions required to connect to the file system's VPC

qualifiers.scope: execution role of a function that uses Amazon EFS
qualifiers.condition: the file system has a user-configured IAM policy

evidence.quote: If the file system has a user-configured IAM policy, your function's execution role must have the correct elasticfilesystem permissions.

These permissions are included in the AmazonElasticFileSystemClientReadWriteAccess managed policy. Additionally, your execution role must have the permissions required to connect to the file system's VPC.
